record.title: Google reports a Gemini 4 Argon workflow porting an ocean model from Fortran to Rust
record.summary: Google Antigravity reports that Gemini 4 Argon migrated the 174,774-line Fortran/C core of FVCOM to safe Rust in a 59-minute run, with 100-seed numerical parity, 42 tests, 96.8% branch coverage, six reported bug findings and 1.88× runtime after optimization. The post gives stage timings and a runtime/memory scorecard, making the account more detailed than a product demo. The run, metrics, exact input correspondence and scientific validity remain first-party and have not been independently reproduced; the linked skill’s immutable source and run artifacts were unavailable in this review.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: Google Antigravity published a detailed account on 3 November 2026 describing a Gemini 4 Argon-assisted migration of FVCOM’s Fortran/C core to Rust.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Google reports that its 59-minute workflow ported 174,774 lines across 264 files, enforced Rust unsafe-code prohibition, passed 42 tests with 96.8% branch coverage, and matched 100 randomized Fortran runs to 12 decimal places.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Google reports six legacy bug findings and a runtime change from 883 ms for the Fortran baseline to 469 ms after Struct-of-Arrays allocation changes and LLVM profile-guided optimization; reported peak memory falls from 11.84 MB to 5.48 MB.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The article does not independently establish the migration metrics, numerical validity across real scientific use, exact correspondence between the public FVCOM revision and run input, or generality to other legacy scientific codebases.

evidence_gaps.description: The public post does not expose the run workspace, full telemetry, or immutable revision of the reusable migration skill; the reported run and metrics remain first-party.
The exact correspondence between Google’s stated 174,774-line input and an immutable FVCOM upstream revision/configuration has not been verified; no independent end-to-end port was run.

brief.importance_rationale: If a workflow can safely modernize large scientific simulations while preserving numerical results and improving runtime, it could materially affect maintenance of legacy scientific software. The score reflects that potential consequence, not the truth or transferability of Google’s first-party run metrics.
limitations: All migration, parity, coverage, bug-finding, safety and speed metrics are reported by Google; no independent reproduction was inspected.
The linked skill’s web index exposes workflow instructions, but direct GitHub tree and raw-file fetches returned cache miss; the immutable skill revision and run artifacts remain unavailable.
Google’s public post identifies FVCOM 5.0.1 upstream but this activation did not establish that the reported 174,774-line input exactly matches that revision or configuration.
A 100-seed parity report and 42 generated tests do not establish scientific validity across all configurations, boundary conditions or real research use.
The reported 1.88× runtime is attributed to combined Rust conversion, allocation changes and LLVM PGO; it is not an isolated model contribution or a general migration speedup.

The post gives stage timings and a runtime/memory scorecard, making the account more detailed than a product demo. technical.claimed_result: Google reports a 59-minute migration of 174,774 lines across 264 FVCOM Fortran/C files, 42 tests with 96.8% branch coverage, 100-seed numerical parity to 12 decimal places and six legacy bug findings. Its scorecard reports 883 ms for the Fortran baseline and 469 ms after Rust, Struct-of-Arrays allocation changes and LLVM PGO; peak memory falls from 11.84 MB to 5.48 MB.
technical.compute_or_cost: The reported agent workflow took 59 minutes (11-minute baseline, 3-minute audit and 45-minute port/optimization). Google provides no model-token, compute-cost, human-labor accounting or independent time measurement.
technical.demonstrated_result: Google published a detailed first-party account including workflow stages, test/parity procedure and a runtime/memory table. The underlying run and all result metrics were not independently inspected or reproduced.
technical.implementation_status: The article says Google released a reusable migrate-to-rust skill. A skills index exposed its instructions, while direct GitHub tree/raw-source fetches failed during this review; the exact skill commit and run workspace were not inspected.
technical.mechanism: The described workflow audits cross-file dependencies, builds a compiled Fortran baseline and golden outputs, creates a migration blueprint, ports the solver into safe Rust modules, runs tests and multi-seed parity checks, then applies LLVM profile-guided optimization.
technical.regime: One reported FVCOM coastal-ocean-model migration; Google identifies 174,774 lines of Fortran 90/C in 264 files. Results use 100 randomized simulation seeds, 42 tests and a specific Fortran -O3 baseline and Rust/PGO configuration. No cross-project generality is demonstrated.
technical.reproducibility: The public article documents steps and headline scorecard values but does not provide the run’s immutable code revision, generated workspace, complete telemetry or independent reproduction. Exact scientific and numerical validation remains open.
technical.strongest_baseline: Google compares its optimized Rust result with a compiled Fortran -O3 baseline on the reported runtime/memory harness and reports parity across 100 seeds. The exact upstream revision and matching test input were not verified.

brief.title: Google reports a Gemini 4 Argon workflow porting an ocean model from Fortran to Rust
brief.why_it_matters: Scientific models often encode decades of validated domain logic in hard-to-maintain software. If this reported workflow can preserve numerical behavior while modernizing such code, it could change maintenance and performance options for scientific computing. Current evidence is a detailed first-party report about one migration; independent reproduction, exact input correspondence and broader validity remain unknown.
